senses: The property of being scrupulous; excessive attention to scruples.
A mental disorder, generally considered a subtype of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), characterized by excessive concern with moral or religious matters
examples: Age looks with anger on the temerity of youth, and youth with contempt on the scrupulosity of age.

senses: To divide into quartiles.
ety: From Middle French quartil, from Medieval Latin quartilus. By surface analysis, quart + -ile.

senses: One who groups things.
Drawn in lines without colours.
A goldish-yellow colour, like that of a lemon.
A brownish-yellow quartz.
ety: From Middle English citrine, partly from Middle French citrine and partly from Latin citrīnus.

senses: An assistant to a bartender.
ety: From bar + back, due to working in the back area of the bar and not interacting with the patrons. Compare back of house and back office.

senses: Any members of family Eupleridae of Malagasy mongooses, only distantly related to the Herpestidae, but resembling them in appearance and habits, with larger ears and ringed tails.
ety: First attested in the 1690s. Borrowed from Portuguese manguço, from Marathi मुंगूस (muṅgūs), from Old Marathi 𑘦𑘳𑘽𑘐𑘳𑘭 (muṃgusa). Ultimately a Dravidian borrowing (compare Telugu ముంగిస (muṅgisa)), from Proto-Dravidian *mūnkūc- (“mongoose”). Spelling altered by folk-etymological association with goose. Displaced native Old English nǣderbita (literally “snake biter”).

senses: A member of the equestrian order (Latin: ordo equester), the lower of the two aristocratic classes of Ancient Rome, ranking below the patricians.
Someone who plays an oboe.
An energetic Japanese style of folk dance.
The unit of currency in Indonesia.
ety: Borrowed from Indonesian rupiah, in turn Borrowed from Pali rūpiya (“silver”), in turn borrowed from Sanskrit रूप्यक (rūpyaka, “a silver coin”), from रूप्य (rūpya, “wrought silver”). Doublet of rupee and rufiyaa.

senses: The formation of small crystals in a glass as a result of slow cooling from the molten state.
A wise person with knowledge of lore in any number of topics, such as history, genealogy, ancient poetry and possibly magic as well; A scholar.
ety: From lore + master, possibly a learned borrowing from Middle English or calque of Middle English lore maistir (“teacher of knowledge”).

senses: Any of many small wasps of the superfamily Chalcidoidea, most of which are parasitoids of other insects.
ety: From New Latin genus name Chalcis, from Ancient Greek Χαλκίς, from χαλκός ("copper", "bronze"), because wasps of that genus have metallic colors on their exoskeletons.

senses: To form (scraps of metal) into ingots.
ety: From Middle English ingot (“mould for casting metal”), of uncertain origin. In all likelihood the same word as Middle French lingot, but the direction of borrowing is hard to establish, particularly as the word appears simultaneously (ca. 1390) in both languages. * Assuming English origin, from Old English ingoten, past participle of inġēotan (“to pour in”), derived from Proto-Germanic *geutaną (“to pour”, whence archaic English yote). Compare Old English ingyte (“a pouring-in, infusion”), which is formed with a related noun (Proto-Germanic *gutiz, whence German Guss, Swedish göt). Also relate

senses: The act of strangling or the state of being strangled.
The constriction of the air passage or other body part that cuts off the flow of a fluid.
ety: From Latin strangulatio (“choking, suffocation”), from strangulare (“to choke, suffocate”); see strangle.

senses: Fat of the back, especially of pigs.
Stir-fried sliced tteoks (Korean rice cakes) seasoned with red pepper paste.
ety: Borrowed from Korean 떡볶이 (tteokbokki), from 떡 (tteok, “rice cake”) + 볶이 (bokki, “stir-fried and seasoned food”).

senses: Displaying a tendency or intent to coerce.
Not quantified (in any sense).
Between zones.
The act of impinging.
The stomach of a hawk.
ety: An old spelling of panel which became standard in falconry.
examples: Glut is the slimy substance that lies in the hawk's pannel.

senses: Characterized by bloat or bloating.
The religion, philosophical beliefs, and attendant ritual practices of the druids.
Used for chewing.
ety: From Latin mastico + -atory, the former borrowed from Ancient Greek μαστιχάω (mastikháō, “I gnash the teeth”), from μάσταξ (mástax, “that with which one chews”).

senses: An Italian liqueur made from elderberries and flavoured with licorice, traditionally served with 3 coffee beans that represent health, wealth and fortune (or past, present and future).
ety: ] Borrowed from Italian sambuca, from Latin sambūcus (“elder tree”), due to a similar 19th century liquor flavored with elderflower. Modern sambuca, which doesn't necessarily have elderberry, started being marketed in 1971.

senses: Having an inclination to commit homicide.
Any system larger than a microcosm but smaller than a macrocosm, especially when used as an outdoor experimental system that examines the natural environment under controlled conditions.
Someone who advocates for these actions.
examples: Over the past two years, particularly in 2018, Network Rail has come under fire about its approaches to trackside tree-felling across its 52,000-hectare estate. Conservationists accused it of wanton destruction.

senses: A kind of ancient poem in Germanic languages, consisting of metrical lists of poetic synonyms for oral recitation.
The study of cutaneous diseases at a microscopic level.
examples: Her father is a professor of pathology at Harvard Medical School and the director of dermatopathology at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston.

senses: A corrupt and dishonest government or society characterised by theft and greed.
A traditional region or local administrative division found in parts of Spain, Portugal, Panama, Nicaragua, and Brazil.
One who, or that which, keys.
A device for signalling by pressing keys or switches.
A device that replaces a fixed colour in the image with some other picture or background; chromakeyer.
An odd, eccentric or insane person.
A bag filled with nuts, especially one that is hung outdoors to act as a bird feeder.
A kind of reciprocating saw, a tool similiar to a thick, long-bladed electric jigsaw used to saw through most things, favored for demolition.
ety: A genericization of the trademark Sawzall.

senses: An armlock where the implementer isolates the opponent's arm and torques the shoulder in order to cause pain or injury.
A digital feature used by disc jockeys that locks a track to its original key regardless of changes made to the tempo.
The thumb; the first, or preaxial, digit of the forelimb, corresponding to the hallux in the hind limb. In birds, the pollex is the joint which bears the alula or bastard wing.
examples: The Simiidae have a man-like appearance. They possess neither tails nor bestial cheek pouches. Their arms are longer than their legs, and they have opposable pollexes and a broad sternum.

Among the crabs with abnormal legs, one leg had two pollexes and three dactyls (Fig. 4B), one had a Y-shaped dactyl (Fig. 4C), two had clawlike dactyls (Fig. 4D), and the rest of the abnormal legs had a curved structure.

senses: Not edifying.
Ungraceful, usually due to a clash of expectations or disparity of knowledge.
examples: Sunday’s scenes were the kind of unedifying thing some of those aggressive members prefer to think only happens in all the sports on which they look down, or during prime minister’s questions.
